string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and a municipality in the north of the country. Its urban history stretches back more than three thousand years, and successive dynasties shaped its streets, palaces, and ceremonial spaces. The Forbidden City preserves the imperial palace of the Ming and Qing periods, while traditional hutongs reveal another side of the old city. Today, Beijing combines this heritage with national institutions, universities, research centres, and modern industries. It serves as a major centre for politics, culture, international exchange, and scientific innovation, connecting a long historical legacy with contemporary urban life.

Shanghai is a municipality on the eastern coast of China, near the mouth of the Yangtze River. Its position in the Yangtze River Delta helped it develop into an important trading city. After its port opened in 1843, commerce and industry expanded, leaving a varied architectural heritage. The Huangpu River divides the central city into Puxi and Pudong, linking the historic waterfront with a modern skyline. Shanghai now plays major roles in finance, shipping, international trade, and technological innovation. Its museums, neighbourhoods, and riverfront spaces show how local traditions and international connections have influenced the city.

Chongqing is a municipality in southwest China along the upper Yangtze River. Its central urban districts occupy hilly ground around the meeting of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers, giving the city its distinctive mountain and river landscape. Chongqing became a municipality directly administered by the central government in 1997. The municipality extends far beyond the central skyline to include other towns, countryside, valleys, and mountainous areas. Jiefangbei, a historic monument surrounded by a busy commercial district, illustrates the relationship between its past and present. Chongqing is also an important regional centre for administration, business, finance, and transport.

Tianjin is a municipality in northern China, where the Haihe River flows towards the Bohai Sea. Its location made it an important connection between inland waterways and maritime trade. A garrison established in 1404 marked a key stage in the development of the city. River transport and commerce subsequently encouraged its growth, and modern Tianjin became a significant industrial, financial, and trading centre. Today, its port links northern China with international shipping routes. Historic streets and waterfront areas reflect earlier periods of development, while the surrounding municipality includes coastal plains, wetlands, and mountain scenery in the north.
